title: Trailing clouds of glory
hook: a Christian poet seems to say the soul lived before birth; we come trailing clouds of glory (Intimations Ode)
tomorrow: some moments come back for years. do they heal you, or haunt you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, getting and spending: Wordsworth by the moonlit sea, ashamed of the trade we've made with our hearts. Today, a stranger question, the kind only children ask out loud.

Kids ask the questions grown-ups quietly stopped asking. Where was I before I was born? Wordsworth's answer comes in a long ode, and it's a puzzle. "Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting", he writes. Birth as falling asleep? Then: "The Soul that rises with us, our life's Star, / Hath had elsewhere its setting, / And cometh from afar". A Christian poet, saying the soul was somewhere before birth? Churches have long rejected that idea. So what is he doing?
screen: `WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?` → `BIRTH IS A SLEEP AND A FORGETTING.` → `THE SOUL COMETH FROM AFAR.` → `WHAT IS HE DOING?`

segments.voice: Wordsworth answered the puzzle himself, in a note he dictated years later. He didn't mean to teach that the soul lived before birth. It was an old notion, he said, and he used it as a poet, because it fit something he knew from childhood. The old notion is Plato's. In the dialogues called the Meno and the Phaedo, Socrates argues that learning is really remembering, anamnesis: the soul knew the truth before birth and forgot it on arrival. Wordsworth borrows the picture, then, a few lines on, turns it toward his own faith: "But trailing clouds of glory do we come / From God, who is our home: / Heaven lies about us in our infancy!" Then the growing up: "Shades of the prison-house begin to close / Upon the growing Boy", until the light fades "into the light of common day." So here's the solution. It isn't a doctrine of past lives. It's a picture of a teaching Christians do hold: we come from God, and we go home to God. Ecclesiastes says it plainly: "the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." Wordsworth borrows Plato to explain why a child sees glory that grown-ups miss. And the ode doesn't end in loss. He says he will grieve not, but find strength in what remains behind.
screen: `A POET'S NOTION, NOT A CREED.` · `PLATO: LEARNING IS REMEMBERING.` · `FROM GOD, WHO IS OUR HOME.` · `THE PRISON-HOUSE CLOSES.` · then, large: `TRAILING CLOUDS OF GLORY.`

segments.voice: Say out loud, quietly, one thing that amazed you as a small child: a snowfall, a beetle, a grandparent's hands. Describe it in a few sentences, as if to someone who has never seen one. Then sit with whatever light comes back.
Trailing clouds of glory: Wordsworth's picture of children arriving from God with heaven still around them. A poet's notion, he said, not a creed.
Keep this: trailing clouds of glory, from God, who is our home. Till next time.
